concepts.title: The kubectl Debugging Workflow: describe, logs, exec
concepts.description: kubectl get, describe, logs, and exec each answer a different, specific question about a broken Pod -- knowing exactly which one to reach for first, and which trap each one has (a stale --previous log, a container that isn't actually Running yet), turns 'my Pod is broken' from a guessing game into a short, repeatable diagnostic sequence.
learningObjectives: Use kubectl get pods to identify which lifecycle stage a broken Pod is stuck in from its STATUS and RESTARTS columns.
Use kubectl describe pod to read the Events section and map specific event reasons to the component and stage responsible.
Use kubectl logs, including --previous and -c, to read a crashed container's own output rather than a fresh restart's near-empty log stream.
Use kubectl exec to inspect a live, Running container's environment, mounted files, and connectivity to a dependency.
Explain why kubectl exec and kubectl logs --previous target fundamentally different moments in a container's lifecycle, and why picking the wrong one wastes time.
Use kubectl port-forward to reach a specific Pod directly, bypassing its Service, to isolate whether a problem is in the Pod or in the networking layer in front of it.

sections.heading: Start With kubectl get pods: The STATUS Column Is a Map
sections.body:
Before reaching for any deeper tool, `kubectl get pods` gives a fast, cheap first read on which *stage* of a Pod's lifecycle is actually broken -- and that answer determines which of the deeper tools is even worth trying next. `Pending` means the Pod hasn't been scheduled yet, or an init container hasn't finished; nothing has started running at all, so `kubectl logs` and `kubectl exec` have nothing to show you yet. `ContainerCreating` means it's been scheduled and the kubelet is working on it (commonly: pulling an image). `ImagePullBackOff`/`ErrImagePull` means the image pull itself is failing (wrong tag, private registry auth, network). `CrashLoopBackOff` means the container starts, then exits, repeatedly, with the kubelet backing off increasingly long delays between restart attempts. `Running` means the container process is currently alive -- which, importantly, says nothing at all about whether the *application* inside it is actually healthy or serving requests correctly.

The `RESTARTS` column is worth reading alongside `STATUS`: a Pod showing `Running` with `RESTARTS: 14` and climbing is not a healthy Pod that happens to say Running right now -- it's a Pod that keeps crashing and getting restarted by the kubelet, currently caught mid-cycle between one crash and the next, and is functionally in the same category of broken as one currently displaying `CrashLoopBackOff`. Treating `Running` as automatically meaning 'fine' is one of the most common ways people waste time investigating the wrong thing first.

sections.heading: kubectl describe pod: Reading the Events Section
sections.body:
`kubectl describe pod <name>` prints the Pod's full spec and status, but the single most useful part for debugging sits at the very bottom: a chronological **Events** table -- the exact same underlying event stream introduced back in the Cluster Architecture concept, filtered to just this one object.

```text
Events:
  Type     Reason     Age   From               Message
  ----     ------     ----  ----               -------
  Normal   Scheduled  2m    default-scheduler  Successfully assigned default/web-abc to node-2
  Normal   Pulling    2m    kubelet            Pulling image "my-app:1.4"
  Normal   Pulled     1m    kubelet            Successfully pulled image "my-app:1.4"
  Normal   Created    1m    kubelet            Created container app
  Normal   Started    1m    kubelet            Started container app
  Warning  Unhealthy  30s   kubelet            Liveness probe failed: HTTP probe failed with statuscode: 500
  Normal   Killing    30s   kubelet            Container app failed liveness probe, will be restarted
  Warning  BackOff    10s   kubelet            Back-off restarting failed container
```

Each `Reason` maps directly onto a specific component and stage from the cluster architecture you already know: `Scheduled` is the scheduler's output; `Pulling`/`Pulled`/`Created`/`Started` are all the kubelet driving the container runtime through its own startup sequence; `FailedScheduling` (not shown above) would mean the scheduler itself couldn't place the Pod at all, with a message like `0/3 nodes are available: 3 Insufficient cpu`. Reading this table top to bottom tells you exactly which stage the Pod actually got stuck at, which is precisely why `describe`, not `logs`, should usually be the *second* command you run (right after `get pods`) -- it tells you whether the problem is even inside the container's own code yet, or happened before the container ever got a chance to run at all.

sections.heading: kubectl logs and the --previous Trap
sections.body:
`kubectl logs <pod>` streams the stdout/stderr of the Pod's (single) container's *current* process. For a Pod stuck in `CrashLoopBackOff`, this is exactly where people most often waste time: the *currently running* container instance is often a fresh restart that has barely started and hasn't reached the code path that crashes yet -- so `kubectl logs` shows little or nothing useful, and it's tempting to conclude 'there's nothing in the logs' when the actual crash's output is sitting one restart back.

`kubectl logs <pod> --previous` (or `-p`) is the fix: it retrieves the logs of the *immediately preceding, already-terminated* container instance -- the one that actually crashed -- rather than the current one that may not have failed yet. This single flag resolves the majority of 'the logs are empty but the Pod is clearly crashing' confusion.

```bash
kubectl logs web-abc123                 # current instance -- may be nearly empty right after a fresh restart
kubectl logs web-abc123 --previous      # the instance that actually crashed
kubectl logs web-abc123 -c sidecar      # multi-container Pod: must name the specific container
kubectl logs web-abc123 -f --tail=50    # follow new output live, starting from the last 50 lines
```

For any Pod with more than one container, `-c <container-name>` is not optional -- `kubectl logs` on a multi-container Pod with no `-c` flag either defaults to the only container (if there's exactly one) or errors out asking you to specify one; it never silently merges multiple containers' logs into one stream.

sections.heading: kubectl exec, Ephemeral Debug Containers, and port-forward
sections.body:
`kubectl exec -it <pod> -- /bin/sh` opens an interactive shell *inside* a specific, currently-**Running** container, letting you check things no external tool can see directly: actual resolved environment variables (`env`), whether a ConfigMap/Secret volume mount actually contains what you expect (`cat /etc/app-config/LOG_LEVEL`), whether the container can reach a dependency at all (`curl -v http://db:5432`, `nslookup db`), or what processes are actually running inside (`ps aux`).

This only works on a container that is genuinely `Running` right now -- it cannot attach to a Pod stuck `Pending`, `ContainerCreating`, or mid-crash in `CrashLoopBackOff` between restart attempts, because there's no live process to attach a shell to at that moment. A second, separate limitation: many production images (especially minimal 'distroless' base images, built deliberately without a shell or package manager to shrink attack surface) have no `/bin/sh` at all, so `kubectl exec` into them fails with 'executable file not found,' not because the container is unhealthy, but because there's genuinely no shell binary to run. `kubectl debug <pod> -it --image=busybox --target=<container>` sidesteps this by attaching a *separate*, throwaway 'ephemeral container' -- one with a real shell -- into the same Pod, sharing its network and (optionally) process namespace, without needing to modify or restart the original container at all.

`kubectl port-forward pod/<name> 8080:80` opens a direct tunnel from your local machine straight to one specific Pod, entirely bypassing any Service, Endpoints, or kube-proxy rewriting in front of it. This is the tool for a very specific, narrow question: 'is the problem inside this one Pod itself, or is it somewhere in the Service/networking layer sitting in front of it?' If curling `localhost:8080` after a port-forward works fine, but the Service is still failing, the bug lives in the selector/Endpoints/kube-proxy layer covered in the Services concept, not in the Pod.

sections.heading: Putting It Together: A Systematic Diagnosis Order
sections.body:
A workable default sequence, in order, for 'this Pod is broken and I don't yet know why': (1) `kubectl get pods` -- read STATUS and RESTARTS to know which stage is broken. (2) `kubectl describe pod` -- read Events bottom-to-top-of-the-clock (i.e. in the order shown) to see exactly where the sequence stalled or what failed. (3) If the container has actually started at least once, `kubectl logs --previous` (and plain `kubectl logs` if it's currently Running and you want to see live behavior) to see what the application itself said. (4) If the container is currently Running and the mystery is still unsolved, `kubectl exec` in to inspect live state directly.

A few common mistakes worth naming explicitly, because each one wastes real time: jumping straight to `kubectl logs` before `describe`, and therefore missing a `FailedScheduling` or `ImagePullBackOff` event that explains the whole problem before the container ever ran any application code at all; forgetting `--previous` on a crash-looping Pod and concluding 'the logs are empty' when they're simply the wrong instance's logs; forgetting `-c <container>` on a multi-container Pod and getting an unhelpful error instead of the log stream you wanted; and trying `kubectl exec` against a Pod that `kubectl get pods` already showed as `Pending` or `CrashLoopBackOff` between restarts, when no live process exists yet to attach to at all.

examples.title: From get to describe: Locating a Scheduling Failure
examples.code:
kubectl get pods
# NAME        READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
# web-abc123  0/1     Pending   0          6m

kubectl describe pod web-abc123 | tail -6
# Events:
#   Type     Reason            Age   From               Message
#   ----     ------            ----  ----               -------
#   Warning  FailedScheduling  6m    default-scheduler  0/3 nodes are available: 3 Insufficient memory.
examples.explanation: STATUS: Pending with 0 RESTARTS and 6 minutes of age is the first strong signal that this Pod never got past the scheduling stage at all -- there's no point running kubectl logs or kubectl exec yet, since no container has ever started. describe pod's Events table confirms exactly why: FailedScheduling, from the scheduler itself, with a message naming the specific constraint (Insufficient memory) that no node could satisfy. This is the same class of failure covered in the Cluster Architecture concept's exercise -- the fix lives in the Pod's resources.requests or the cluster's available node capacity, not in anything log- or exec-related, because the container has genuinely never run.

examples.title: The --previous Flag Revealing an Otherwise-Invisible Crash
examples.code:
kubectl get pods
# NAME        READY   STATUS             RESTARTS   AGE
# web-abc123  0/1     CrashLoopBackOff   5          3m

kubectl logs web-abc123
# (empty -- the current instance restarted seconds ago and hasn't reached the crash point yet)

kubectl logs web-abc123 --previous
# Traceback (most recent call last):
#   File "app.py", line 12, in <module>
#     db = connect(os.environ["DATABASE_URL"])
# KeyError: 'DATABASE_URL'
examples.explanation: The plain kubectl logs call looks like a dead end -- no output at all -- which is exactly the trap this concept warns about: the current container instance is a fresh restart that simply hasn't run long enough to hit the crashing code path again yet. Adding --previous retrieves the logs from the instance one restart back -- the one that actually crashed -- and immediately reveals the real cause: the application is reading os.environ["DATABASE_URL"] and finding it unset, a KeyError that kills the process on every single startup. This points straight at a missing environment variable, most likely an envFrom/configMapKeyRef reference that was left out of the Deployment's Pod template, tying directly back to the ConfigMaps and Secrets concept.

examples.title: kubectl exec to Verify a Mounted Secret, and kubectl debug for a Shell-less Image
examples.code:
kubectl exec -it web-abc123 -- sh -c 'ls /etc/secrets && cat /etc/secrets/password | wc -c'
# password
# 0
# -- the file exists but is empty: the Secret key is probably missing or misnamed, not a mount-path problem

# Against a distroless image with no shell at all:
kubectl exec -it web-abc123 -- sh
# OCI runtime exec failed: exec failed: unable to start container process: exec: "sh": executable file not found in $PATH

kubectl debug -it web-abc123 --image=busybox --target=app
# (attaches a separate, throwaway container with a real shell into the same Pod,
#  sharing its network namespace, letting you curl localhost or inspect /proc/<pid>/root)
examples.explanation: The first command uses exec to answer a question no external tool could answer directly: is the Secret volume actually mounted, and does the file inside it actually have content? Finding an empty file (0 bytes) rules out 'the volume isn't mounted at all' and instead points at the Secret itself being empty or the wrong key being referenced in the volume's items list. The second and third commands show the shell-less-image failure mode and its fix: a distroless or otherwise minimal image has no sh binary for exec to run at all, so the fix isn't to keep retrying exec -- it's to attach a separate ephemeral debug container via kubectl debug, which brings its own shell along without touching the original container's image.

misconceptions.description: kubectl logs <pod> always shows whatever caused the container's most recent crash, since that's clearly the most relevant thing that happened to it recently.
misconceptions.clarification: kubectl logs with no flags shows the CURRENT container instance's output -- and for a Pod that's actively crash-looping, the current instance is very often a fresh restart that hasn't yet run long enough to reach whatever code path crashes, so its own log output can be empty or unhelpful even though the Pod is clearly, repeatedly failing. The actual crash's output belongs to the PREVIOUS, already-terminated instance, retrievable specifically via kubectl logs --previous -- treating a lack of output from the plain command as 'there's nothing to see here' is one of the most common time-wasting mistakes in Kubernetes debugging.

misconceptions.description: kubectl exec will work on any Pod that shows up in kubectl get pods, since the Pod obviously exists.
misconceptions.clarification: kubectl exec requires a specific container to currently be in the Running state with a live process the shell can attach to -- it will fail against a Pod stuck Pending or ContainerCreating (nothing has started yet) and will fail against a Pod caught between restart attempts in CrashLoopBackOff (the previous process already exited and the next one hasn't started yet). It can also fail against a Pod that IS genuinely Running, if that container's image has no shell binary at all (common in minimal/distroless images) -- in which case the fix is kubectl debug with an ephemeral debug container, not repeatedly retrying exec against the original container.

exercises.prompt: A Pod shows `STATUS: CrashLoopBackOff` and `RESTARTS: 8`. `kubectl describe pod` shows Events ending in `Liveness probe failed` followed by `Killing` and `BackOff`. `kubectl logs <pod>` shows nothing useful. What single next command is most likely to reveal the actual application-level error, and why would plain `kubectl logs` (without that addition) keep failing to show it?
exercises.code:
kubectl get pods
# web-abc123   0/1   CrashLoopBackOff   8   4m

kubectl logs web-abc123
# (empty or unhelpful)
hints: The container currently running is very likely a fresh restart -- how much time has it had to reach whatever code path is actually failing?
There's a specific flag for retrieving the logs of the container instance that existed immediately before the current one.
The failing instance's own output is not gone -- it's just not the one kubectl logs shows you by default.
exercises.expectedAnswer: kubectl logs web-abc123 --previous. The currently running instance is a fresh restart that likely hasn't yet reached the point where it fails again, so its own logs are sparse or empty; --previous retrieves the logs of the immediately preceding, already-terminated instance -- the one that actually crashed -- which is where the real error message will be.
exercises.solutionExplanation: With RESTARTS climbing and the events showing repeated liveness-probe-triggered kills, this container is caught in a genuine crash loop, and the kubelet's back-off delay means the current instance may be quite young -- possibly too young to have reached the failure again. kubectl logs targets only the current instance by default, which is exactly why it's empty here: the real crash output belongs to the previous instance. kubectl logs web-abc123 --previous retrieves that previous, terminated instance's own stdout/stderr specifically, which is where whatever caused the original liveness failure (an unhandled exception, a fatal startup error, an OOM-adjacent slowdown) would actually be visible.

exercises.prompt: A script used during incidents always fails with 'error: a container name must be specified' whenever it's run against this particular Pod, even though it works fine against other, simpler Pods. Find and fix the bug.
hints: This specific error only happens against Pods with more than one container -- what does the app-pod-xyz Pod's spec likely contain that a simpler Pod's doesn't?
kubectl logs has no default behavior of picking 'the main one' or merging multiple containers' output for you.
The fix is adding a flag that names exactly one container to read logs from.
exercises.solutionCode:
kubectl get pod app-pod-xyz -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[*].name}'
# app  log-shipper

kubectl logs app-pod-xyz -c app
exercises.solutionExplanation: This error specifically means the target Pod has multiple containers (likely a main app container plus a sidecar, such as a log shipper), and kubectl logs refuses to guess which one you meant -- unlike a single-container Pod, where it has an unambiguous default. The fix is to first list the Pod's container names (via kubectl get pod ... -o jsonpath, or kubectl describe pod) and then supply -c <container-name> to kubectl logs to specify exactly which container's stream to read. This is precisely the multi-container-Pod detail introduced back in the Pods concept -- a Pod's containers are independent processes with independent log streams, and nothing about being in the same Pod merges them into one.

assessments.prompt: A Pod shows `STATUS: Pending` with `RESTARTS: 0` and has been in that state for 10 minutes. What is the most appropriate next debugging command, and why?
options: kubectl exec -it <pod> -- sh, to inspect the container's environment directly.
kubectl logs <pod> --previous, to see what caused the most recent crash.
kubectl describe pod <pod>, to read the Events section and see why the Pod hasn't been scheduled or started yet.
kubectl port-forward pod/<pod> 8080:80, to test connectivity directly against the Pod.
assessments.explanation: Pending with zero restarts means no container in this Pod has ever actually started running -- there is no live process to exec into (ruling out option A), no previous crashed instance to retrieve logs from since nothing has run at all (ruling out option B), and nothing listening on any port to forward traffic to (ruling out option D). kubectl describe pod's Events section is exactly the tool for this stage, since it will surface either a scheduling failure (FailedScheduling, with a specific resource or constraint named) or show that an init container is still running or stuck -- either way, revealing why the Pod hasn't progressed past Pending, which is the actual question at this stage.

assessments.prompt: Walk through, in order, the full diagnostic sequence you'd use for a Pod reported as 'broken' with no other information given, explaining what question each command answers and why the order matters.
assessments.modelAnswer: The first command is always kubectl get pods, specifically to read the STATUS and RESTARTS columns -- this is the cheapest possible check and it immediately narrows down which lifecycle stage is actually broken: never-scheduled (Pending), image-pull failure (ImagePullBackOff), repeated crashing (CrashLoopBackOff or a climbing RESTARTS count even while showing Running), or genuinely Running with an application-level problem that isn't visible at this level at all. The second command is kubectl describe pod, read specifically for its Events section at the bottom -- this answers 'at which specific stage, by which specific component, did things go wrong,' since each event Reason (FailedScheduling, Pulling/Pulled, Started, Unhealthy, BackOff) maps onto a distinct part of the pipeline covered in the Cluster Architecture concept. This step matters before touching logs or exec because it can resolve the whole question immediately if the Pod never even got far enough to run application code -- a scheduling failure or an image pull problem has nothing to do with anything inside the container, and reaching for logs or exec first would be looking in the wrong place entirely. Only once describe confirms the container has actually started at least once does kubectl logs --previous (for a Pod that has crashed at least once) or plain kubectl logs (for a Pod that's Running and you want to see current behavior) become the right next step, since it's specifically the application's own stdout/stderr that can explain a logic-level failure the platform-level tools can't see. Finally, if the container is currently Running and the mystery still isn't solved by logs alone, kubectl exec lets you inspect live state directly -- actual resolved environment variables, actual file contents under a mounted volume, actual connectivity to a dependency -- which is the most expensive and most invasive tool of the four, and therefore the one reached for last, only once the cheaper checks have narrowed down that the problem is something exec can actually help answer.

concepts.title: Liveness vs. Readiness Probes
concepts.description: A liveness probe answers 'should this container be killed and restarted' while a readiness probe answers 'should this Pod currently receive traffic' -- two entirely different questions with two entirely different consequences, and conflating them is one of the most common ways teams accidentally cause their own crash loops or route requests to Pods that can't handle them yet.
learningObjectives: Explain precisely what a liveness probe controls (kubelet-initiated container restart) versus what a readiness probe controls (Service Endpoints membership), and why conflating them causes real incidents.
Configure httpGet, exec, and tcpSocket probe types, and choose the right one for a given application.
Explain the role of initialDelaySeconds, periodSeconds, timeoutSeconds, and failureThreshold, and predict how misconfiguring them induces a crash loop under load.
Explain how a startupProbe interacts with a liveness probe for slow-starting applications, and why omitting one is a common cause of false-positive restarts.
Predict, for a given probe configuration and application behavior, whether a struggling Pod gets restarted, gets removed from Service traffic, or both.
Debug a Pod that's Running but receiving no traffic by inspecting its readiness probe configuration and its Service's Endpoints.

sections.heading: Two Different Questions, Two Different Consequences
sections.body:
A **liveness probe** answers exactly one question, repeatedly, for the lifetime of a container: 'is this process stuck, deadlocked, or otherwise broken beyond its own ability to recover?' If it fails enough consecutive times, the kubelet's response is destructive and decisive -- it kills the container and restarts it, exactly as if the process had crashed on its own, incrementing the Pod's restart count.

A **readiness probe** answers a completely different question: 'is this container, right now, in a state where it should receive requests?' Its consequence is non-destructive: a failing readiness probe does not touch the container at all -- it keeps running, untouched -- it only removes the Pod from the Endpoints/EndpointSlice object backing any Service that selects it (exactly the mechanism from the Services concept), so traffic simply stops being routed there until readiness starts passing again.

This distinction is the single most important thing to internalize about probes, because the two failure modes look completely different in practice and call for completely different fixes. A container being killed and restarted over and over is a liveness problem (or a genuine application crash). A container that's alive, stable, RESTARTS: 0, but a Service pointed at it has empty Endpoints, is a readiness problem -- and reaching for a liveness-shaped fix (like adjusting restart behavior) for a readiness-shaped symptom, or vice versa, wastes real debugging time precisely because you're solving the wrong mechanism.

sections.heading: Probe Types: httpGet, exec, tcpSocket
sections.body:
All three probe types are configurable identically for either a livenessProbe or a readinessProbe -- the mechanism for checking is the same regardless of what you do with the result.

```yaml
livenessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /healthz
    port: 8080
  initialDelaySeconds: 10
  periodSeconds: 10

readinessProbe:
  exec:
    command: ["cat", "/tmp/ready"]
  periodSeconds: 5

# A third type, for anything that isn't HTTP and doesn't need a custom script:
livenessProbe:
  tcpSocket:
    port: 5432
  periodSeconds: 10
```

`httpGet` issues an HTTP GET against the given path and port, and treats any response in the 200-399 range as success -- this is the natural fit for anything already exposing an HTTP server, since most frameworks make adding a dedicated `/healthz` or `/ready` endpoint cheap. `exec` runs an arbitrary command *inside* the container and treats exit code 0 as success -- useful when readiness genuinely depends on something an HTTP endpoint can't easily express (checking a file's existence, running a small script that checks multiple internal conditions). `tcpSocket` merely attempts to open a TCP connection to the given port and treats a successful connection as success, with no awareness of anything at the application layer above that -- appropriate for services that don't speak HTTP at all (a raw TCP protocol, a database), but also the weakest signal of the three, since a port accepting connections says nothing about whether the process behind it is actually functioning correctly.

sections.heading: The Timing Knobs and the Classic Misconfiguration
sections.body:
Every probe shares the same timing fields: `initialDelaySeconds` (how long to wait after the container starts before the first check), `periodSeconds` (how often to repeat), `timeoutSeconds` (how long a single check attempt is allowed to take before counting as a failure), and `failureThreshold`/`successThreshold` (how many consecutive failures or successes are needed to actually flip the reported state).

Here's the classic, genuinely common bug: a liveness probe configured with `timeoutSeconds: 1` and `failureThreshold: 1`, pointed at an endpoint that's normally fast but occasionally takes 2-3 seconds under real load (a GC pause, a brief spike in concurrent requests, a slow downstream call the health-check handler happens to touch). Under load -- precisely the moment the application is most likely to be legitimately busy rather than actually broken -- the probe times out, the kubelet counts that as a liveness failure, and with `failureThreshold: 1` a single slow response is enough to get the container killed and restarted. The application wasn't unresponsive; the probe's own timing was simply too tight for a perfectly normal, transient slowdown. Restarting a healthy-but-momentarily-slow container doesn't fix anything -- it interrupts in-flight requests and, if the load causing the slowness persists, the new container may hit the exact same slow window shortly after starting, producing a self-inflicted crash loop with a root cause that's entirely the probe's own configuration, not a bug in the application. The fix is straightforward once diagnosed: give liveness probes a materially looser `timeoutSeconds` and a `failureThreshold` of at least 3, since liveness should only fire for a *sustained* failure to respond, not a single slow tick.

sections.heading: startupProbe: Protecting Slow-Starting Apps From Their Own Liveness Probe
sections.body:
Before `startupProbe` existed, the workaround for an application with a long, variable startup time (a JVM warming up, a large in-memory cache being populated, a set of migrations running) was to set a very large `initialDelaySeconds` on the liveness probe itself -- but that has an unwanted side effect: it also delays how quickly a *genuinely* hung application, well past its normal startup window, gets detected and restarted, since liveness checks don't even begin until that whole delay has elapsed.

```yaml
startupProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /healthz
    port: 8080
  failureThreshold: 30
  periodSeconds: 10   # allows up to 300s (30 * 10s) for startup
livenessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /healthz
    port: 8080
  periodSeconds: 5
  failureThreshold: 3  # tight and fast, but only once startupProbe has succeeded
```

`startupProbe` runs first, on its own schedule, and specifically **disables** both the liveness and readiness probes until it succeeds at least once -- once it does, it stops running entirely, and liveness/readiness take over on their own configured schedules from that point forward. This gets the best of both settings: a generous, tolerant budget for the genuinely variable startup phase (`failureThreshold: 30` at `periodSeconds: 10` here permits up to 5 minutes), and a tight, fast liveness probe (`failureThreshold: 3` at `periodSeconds: 5`, roughly 15 seconds to detect a real hang) once the application has actually finished starting and any slowness after that point is far more likely to indicate a genuine problem worth restarting for.

sections.heading: Readiness Misconfiguration: Traffic to Unready Pods, or Perpetually Excluded Pods
sections.body:
Readiness misconfiguration fails in two opposite directions, and both are common. The first: **no readiness probe defined at all**. Without one, a Pod is considered Ready as soon as its containers are Running -- with zero regard for whether the application has actually finished its own warm-up (loading a cache, opening a database connection pool, registering with something else). A Service pointed at such a Pod will happily route real traffic to it the instant it's Running, even if the application would immediately error or hang on that first request. This is exactly the gap flagged as a footgun back in the Services concept, and it's the reason nearly every production workload should define an explicit readinessProbe rather than relying on the Running-implies-Ready default.

The second direction: a readiness probe that checks something **too strict, or unrelated to this specific Pod's own ability to serve traffic**. A common example is a readiness check that pings a downstream dependency (a third-party API, a shared cache) that's occasionally flaky for reasons that have nothing to do with this Pod's own health -- every one of that Service's Pods bounces in and out of Ready in near-lockstep whenever that shared dependency hiccups, needlessly cutting the Service's actual serving capacity for a problem that a per-Pod readiness check was never well-suited to detect or fix in the first place (a shared dependency being down affects every Pod equally; it's not information about *this* Pod being unhealthy relative to its siblings). The general guidance: readiness should check whether *this specific process* is currently able to do its job -- its own internal state, not the transitive health of everything it happens to talk to.

examples.title: Distinct Liveness and Readiness Endpoints on One Container
examples.code:
containers:
  - name: app
    image: my-app:1.4
    ports:
      - containerPort: 8080
    livenessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /healthz     # "is the process itself alive and not deadlocked?"
        port: 8080
      periodSeconds: 10
      timeoutSeconds: 3
      failureThreshold: 3
    readinessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /ready        # "can I currently serve real requests?"
        port: 8080
      periodSeconds: 5
      timeoutSeconds: 2
      failureThreshold: 2
examples.explanation: Deliberately using two different endpoints lets each probe check exactly what it's meant to check. /healthz might do almost nothing beyond confirming the process can respond at all -- deliberately shallow, so it stays fast and reliable and only fails for a genuinely stuck process, since failing it is destructive. /ready might check that the database connection pool is initialized and a startup cache warm-up has completed -- deliberately stricter, because failing it just quietly excludes the Pod from traffic without hurting anything, which is a far safer default action for a marginal or uncertain state than restarting the container outright. Pointing both probes at the same endpoint with the same thresholds throws away this distinction entirely, and risks treating a readiness-shaped problem (temporarily can't serve requests) as a liveness-shaped one (kill and restart), which is a much more disruptive response than the situation actually calls for.

examples.title: A Liveness Probe Misconfiguration Inducing a Self-Caused Crash Loop
examples.code:
# livenessProbe: httpGet /healthz, timeoutSeconds: 1, periodSeconds: 5, failureThreshold: 1

kubectl describe pod web-abc123 | tail -8
# Events:
#   Warning  Unhealthy  40s (x1 over 40s)  kubelet  Liveness probe failed: Get "http://10.244.1.9:8080/healthz": context deadline exceeded
#   Normal   Killing    40s                kubelet  Container app failed liveness probe, will be restarted
#   Normal   Started    38s                kubelet  Started container app
#   Warning  Unhealthy  10s                kubelet  Liveness probe failed: Get "http://10.244.1.9:8080/healthz": context deadline exceeded
#   Normal   Killing    10s                kubelet  Container app failed liveness probe, will be restarted
examples.explanation: With timeoutSeconds: 1 and failureThreshold: 1, a single HTTP response that takes longer than one second is enough, on its own, to trigger a kill-and-restart -- there's no tolerance for even one transient slow tick. If the application is under real load and its /healthz handler (even a cheap one) occasionally takes 1.2 seconds because of scheduling delay or GC pause, this configuration restarts a perfectly functional container purely because of the load, not because anything is actually broken -- and if that same load persists across the restart, the new container may hit the same timeout again shortly after starting, producing exactly the repeating pattern shown here. The fix is loosening timeoutSeconds (to something like 3-5s) and raising failureThreshold to at least 3, so only a sustained, repeated failure to respond -- not one slow tick -- triggers a restart.

examples.title: startupProbe Giving a Slow-Starting App Room, Without Weakening Liveness Afterward
examples.code:
# WITHOUT startupProbe: liveness alone, forced to compromise
# livenessProbe: initialDelaySeconds: 120 (guesses the worst-case startup time),
#                periodSeconds: 5, failureThreshold: 3
# -- a genuine post-startup hang now takes up to 120s (the fixed delay) before
#    even the FIRST check happens, then another ~15s of failures to detect it.

# WITH startupProbe: the two concerns are separated
# startupProbe:  failureThreshold: 30, periodSeconds: 10   (up to 300s to start)
# livenessProbe: periodSeconds: 5,  failureThreshold: 3    (only ~15s to detect a hang, but ONLY once startupProbe has already succeeded once)

kubectl describe pod web-abc123 | grep -A2 "Started container\|Startup probe"
# Normal  Started        4m10s  kubelet  Started container app
# Normal  Killing        4m5s   kubelet  Startup probe failed: ... (retried, still within budget)
# Normal  ProbeSucceeded 45s    kubelet  Startup probe succeeded -- liveness/readiness now active
examples.explanation: In the without-startupProbe version, the fixed 120-second initialDelaySeconds has to be large enough to cover the worst-case startup time this application has ever shown, which means a genuine hang occurring shortly after that 120-second mark still isn't caught for a while, since the delay is a flat, unconditional wait applied every single time regardless of whether the app actually needed it. In the with-startupProbe version, the startup phase gets its own generous, repeatedly-checked budget (up to 300 seconds here, but ending the moment the app actually becomes healthy, not waiting out a fixed timer regardless), and liveness only begins ticking on its own tight, fast schedule once startup has genuinely finished -- so a real post-startup hang is caught in roughly 15 seconds rather than being entangled with however long the worst-case cold start happens to take.

misconceptions.description: Liveness and readiness probes are essentially the same mechanism used at two different moments -- pointing both at the same endpoint with the same settings gives you full protection either way.
misconceptions.clarification: They have fundamentally different consequences on failure: a failed liveness probe destroys and restarts the container; a failed readiness probe just excludes the Pod from Service traffic while leaving it running untouched. Because the consequences differ so much, what each probe SHOULD check often differs too -- liveness should verify something narrow like 'is the process itself responsive at all,' since failing it is destructive and should only happen for a genuinely stuck process, while readiness can reasonably check stricter, more application-specific conditions (a warm cache, an open DB pool) since failing it only pauses traffic rather than killing anything. Pointing a liveness probe at a check that's appropriate for readiness (like a downstream dependency ping) risks destructively restarting a perfectly healthy container over a problem restarting it can't even fix.

misconceptions.description: A container that fails its liveness probe gets restarted, but it stays counted as a normal Service backend the whole time, since only readiness failures affect traffic routing.
misconceptions.clarification: In practice a liveness failure does also affect traffic, just indirectly rather than as its primary mechanism: once the kubelet kills the container, the Pod's containers are no longer all Running, so the Pod is no longer Ready either, and it drops out of the Service's Endpoints for the duration of the restart -- readiness and the container's actual running state are linked, since a killed container obviously can't be genuinely ready to serve anything. The distinction that actually matters is which mechanism is doing the excluding and why: a readiness failure alone (container still Running, just reported not-ready) removes a Pod from traffic non-destructively and reversibly the moment readiness passes again; a liveness failure removes it from traffic only as a side effect of the more disruptive act of killing and restarting the container entirely.

exercises.prompt: A Deployment's Pod template defines a livenessProbe but no readinessProbe at all. The application takes about 20 seconds after the container starts to finish connecting to its database, and would error on any request received before that. What happens to traffic sent to this Pod via its Service in the first 20 seconds after the container reaches the Running state?
exercises.code:
containers:
  - name: app
    image: my-app:1.0
    livenessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /healthz
        port: 8080
      initialDelaySeconds: 5
    # no readinessProbe defined
hints: With no readinessProbe at all, what does a Pod's Ready condition default to, based purely on its containers' Running state?
Endpoints/EndpointSlice membership is driven by the Ready condition -- not by whether a readinessProbe exists, and not by anything the liveness probe is checking.
The 20-second database connection window is invisible to Kubernetes entirely if nothing is explicitly checking for it.
exercises.expectedAnswer: The Pod is considered Ready as soon as its container is Running (the default with no readinessProbe), so the Service adds it to Endpoints and starts routing real traffic to it immediately -- including during the 20-second window before its database connection is actually ready, during which any request it receives will error.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Without a readinessProbe, Kubernetes has no configured way to know that this application needs roughly 20 seconds after starting before it can genuinely handle requests -- the only thing being checked is liveness, and even that doesn't start until initialDelaySeconds: 5 has elapsed, and it's checking a completely different thing (process responsiveness) than 'is the DB connection ready.' With no readiness signal defined at all, the Pod's Ready condition defaults to true the moment its container reaches Running, so it's added to the Service's Endpoints immediately and starts receiving real traffic well before the 20-second warm-up finishes, producing exactly the class of request errors this concept describes. The fix is adding a readinessProbe (an httpGet against a /ready endpoint the app only reports healthy on once its DB connection is actually established, for example) so the Pod is correctly excluded from traffic during that specific window.

exercises.prompt: This Deployment's Pods keep entering CrashLoopBackOff under moderate load, even though application-level logs (from kubectl logs --previous) show no errors or crashes at all -- just normal request handling right up until the container is killed. Find and fix the bug.
exercises.code:
livenessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /healthz
    port: 8080
  periodSeconds: 5
  timeoutSeconds: 1
  failureThreshold: 1
hints: If the application's own logs show no crash or error at all, the thing actually killing the container might not be the application's own code.
timeoutSeconds: 1 combined with failureThreshold: 1 means exactly how much tolerance for a single slow response, under any amount of load?
The fix should loosen the probe's own tolerance for transient slowness, not change anything about the application.
exercises.solutionCode:
livenessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /healthz
    port: 8080
  periodSeconds: 5
  timeoutSeconds: 3
  failureThreshold: 3
exercises.solutionExplanation: Clean application logs with no crash, paired with restarts that clearly correspond to Killing/Unhealthy events in kubectl describe pod, points squarely at the liveness probe itself as the thing destroying otherwise-healthy containers -- and timeoutSeconds: 1 with failureThreshold: 1 means a single HTTP response taking just over one second, which is exactly the kind of transient slowdown moderate load can easily cause, is enough on its own to count as a liveness failure and trigger an immediate kill-and-restart. Raising timeoutSeconds to 3 gives each individual check meaningfully more headroom before it's even counted as failed, and raising failureThreshold to 3 additionally requires three consecutive failures (roughly 15 seconds of sustained unresponsiveness at periodSeconds: 5) before a restart is triggered, rather than one isolated slow tick -- converting the probe from something that reacts to normal load variance into something that only reacts to a genuinely sustained hang, which is what a liveness probe should be checking for in the first place.

assessments.prompt: A Pod's readiness probe starts failing repeatedly while its liveness probe continues to pass. What happens to this Pod?
options: The kubelet restarts the container, since any failing probe eventually triggers a restart.
The Pod is deleted entirely and a replacement is scheduled by its controller.
The container keeps running untouched, but the Pod is removed from any Service's Endpoints until readiness starts passing again.
Nothing happens at all -- only liveness probe results have any observable effect on the cluster.
assessments.explanation: A failing readiness probe, on its own, never triggers a restart or a deletion -- its entire effect is on Service routing: the Pod is excluded from the relevant Endpoints/EndpointSlice objects, so kube-proxy stops sending it new traffic, while the container itself keeps running completely untouched, and can resume receiving traffic automatically the moment readiness starts passing again. Option A conflates the two probe types' consequences -- only a failing liveness probe causes a restart. Option B describes something no probe on its own ever does (that's a controller/replica-count concern, unrelated to probe results). Option D is false and is exactly the misconception this concept corrects -- a failing readiness probe absolutely has an observable effect, just a non-destructive, traffic-routing one rather than a restart.

assessments.prompt: A team's Pods are crash-looping under moderate production load, but the application's own logs show no errors. They suspect the liveness probe. Explain, mechanistically, how a liveness probe misconfiguration alone can produce exactly this symptom, and what specifically about the probe's configuration needs to change.
assessments.modelAnswer: A liveness probe's entire job is to answer 'should this container be killed and restarted,' and it makes that decision purely from its own configured timing -- timeoutSeconds (how long one check attempt is allowed to take before it's counted as failed) and failureThreshold (how many consecutive failures are required before the kubelet actually acts). If those values are set too tightly relative to the application's genuine, healthy response-time variance under real load -- for example, timeoutSeconds: 1 with failureThreshold: 1 -- then a single HTTP health check that happens to take 1.2 seconds because the process is legitimately busy handling a burst of real requests (a GC pause, scheduling contention, a momentarily slow downstream call inside the health-check handler itself) is treated exactly the same as a genuinely hung, broken process: the kubelet kills the container and restarts it. This explains the specific symptom described perfectly -- the application's own logs show no error at all, because there genuinely was no application-level bug; the process was doing its job correctly the whole time, just slightly slower than the probe's own timeout tolerated, and it was the platform, not the application, that decided to kill it. Under continued load, the newly restarted container can easily hit the same brief slow window again shortly after starting, producing a repeating crash loop whose actual root cause is entirely in the probe's own timing configuration, not in the application. The fix is to loosen both dimensions of tolerance: increase timeoutSeconds enough to comfortably cover the application's normal (not just best-case) response time under real load, and increase failureThreshold to require several consecutive failures -- not just one -- before treating the situation as a genuine hang worth the disruption of a restart. The general principle underneath the fix is that a liveness probe should only fire for sustained unresponsiveness, since its response (killing the container) is destructive and should be reserved for situations a restart can actually be expected to fix, which a single transient slow tick under normal load is not.

concepts.title: Resource Requests and Limits
concepts.description: requests and limits look like a matched pair of the same kind of setting, but they're enforced by entirely different mechanisms at entirely different times -- requests steer the scheduler's placement decision, while limits are enforced by the kernel at runtime, and understanding exactly why memory limit violations get a container killed (OOMKilled) while CPU limit violations only get it throttled is the key to diagnosing 'my Pod died' versus 'my Pod is just slow' correctly.
learningObjectives: Distinguish what requests are used for (scheduling placement) from what limits are used for (runtime enforcement).
Explain precisely why exceeding a memory limit gets a container OOMKilled, while exceeding a CPU limit only throttles it, tracing the difference to compressible versus incompressible resources.
Describe the three QoS classes (Guaranteed, Burstable, BestEffort), how each is derived automatically from a Pod's requests/limits, and their consequence for node-pressure eviction order.
Read kubectl describe pod output to distinguish an OOMKilled Pod from a CPU-throttled-but-otherwise-healthy Pod.
Explain the purpose of a namespace-level LimitRange and the risk it mitigates when a Pod spec omits resources entirely.
Predict the practical consequence, across many Pods on a node, of setting limits far above requests (overcommit) versus setting requests equal to limits everywhere.

sections.heading: Requests: What the Scheduler Actually Uses
sections.body:
`resources.requests` on a container is a claim used at exactly one moment: when the scheduler is deciding which node a Pod can go on. The scheduler sums up the requests of every Pod already assigned to a node and only considers that node a valid placement if it has enough *unallocated* capacity left to cover the new Pod's requests too -- this is precisely the mechanism behind the `0/3 nodes are available: 3 Insufficient cpu` scheduling failure covered back in the Cluster Architecture concept. Once a Pod is actually scheduled, requests have no further runtime effect at all -- they don't get enforced or checked again; they were purely an input to one placement decision that already happened.

A container with **no `requests` set at all** is treated as requesting effectively nothing, from the scheduler's point of view -- which sounds harmless but is actually a real risk: the scheduler will happily stack such a Pod onto a node with the assumption that it needs zero reserved capacity, even if it goes on to use a meaningful amount of real CPU or memory once running. Enough unrequested Pods landing on the same node this way is exactly how a node ends up genuinely overcommitted -- more real usage than capacity -- despite every individual scheduling decision looking, on paper, like it fit fine.

sections.heading: Limits: Enforced at Runtime by the Kernel, Not the Scheduler
sections.body:
`resources.limits`, by contrast, has nothing to do with the scheduler at all. When the kubelet actually starts a container, it configures the node's cgroup (control group) settings for that specific container's process according to its `limits` -- a purely local, per-node, per-container mechanism, enforced continuously by the kernel for as long as the container runs, completely independent of whatever the scheduler decided beforehand.

This is worth stating plainly because it corrects a natural but wrong assumption: nothing about `limits` involves the API server checking anything on an ongoing basis, and nothing about it involves any component other than the kubelet and the container runtime on that one specific node. A Pod can be scheduled successfully (a `requests`-driven decision, made once, by the scheduler) and then have its containers throttled or killed repeatedly afterward (a `limits`-driven outcome, enforced continuously, by the kernel) -- these are two entirely separate mechanisms operating at two entirely separate times, and a Pod's ongoing health after scheduling has nothing more to do with the scheduler at all.

sections.heading: Why Memory Limits Kill and CPU Limits Throttle
sections.body:
This is the single most commonly confused fact in this entire topic, and it comes down to one property: **memory is incompressible; CPU time is compressible.**

Memory cannot be 'slowed down' -- a process either has the RAM it's currently holding, or it doesn't; there's no way to make a process use less memory right now without actually freeing something, which is not a decision the kernel can force on an application's behalf. So when a container's memory usage hits its cgroup limit, and the process tries to allocate more anyway, the kernel's OOM killer intervenes and terminates the process outright with `SIGKILL`. Kubernetes surfaces this specifically: `kubectl describe pod` shows `Last State: Terminated`, `Reason: OOMKilled`, `Exit Code: 137` (137 is the Unix convention of 128 + signal number, and SIGKILL is signal 9: 128 + 9 = 137). This is a hard, immediate, destructive stop -- there's no warning period and no gradual degradation.

CPU, by contrast, is fundamentally about *time slices*, and time slices can absolutely be withheld without killing anything. The kernel's CFS (Completely Fair Scheduler) bandwidth controller, which is how CPU limits are actually enforced, tracks how much CPU time a container's cgroup has consumed within each fixed accounting period (typically 100ms), and once that quota for the current period is exhausted, the container's processes are simply *not scheduled for any more CPU time* until the next period begins -- they keep existing, keep their memory, keep every bit of state, and simply run slower, in short, repeated pauses. Kubernetes calls this **throttling**, and critically, a throttled container never shows up as `OOMKilled`, never gets restarted because of it, and its RESTARTS count doesn't move at all from CPU throttling alone -- it just quietly, and often invisibly to a quick glance, takes longer to do everything.

```yaml
resources:
  requests:
    cpu: 250m
    memory: 256Mi
  limits:
    cpu: 500m      # exceeding this: throttled, not killed
    memory: 512Mi   # exceeding this: OOMKilled (SIGKILL, exit 137)
```

sections.heading: QoS Classes: Guaranteed, Burstable, BestEffort
sections.body:
Kubernetes automatically derives a **Quality of Service (QoS) class** for every Pod, purely from the shape of its containers' requests and limits -- there is no field you set directly for this; it's computed.

**Guaranteed**: every container in the Pod has `requests` set equal to `limits`, for both CPU and memory. **Burstable**: at least one container has a `requests` set, but not every container has requests exactly equal to limits for both resources (the common, realistic middle case: some slack between what's reserved and what's allowed). **BestEffort**: no container in the Pod sets any requests or limits at all.

This classification matters concretely during **node-pressure eviction** -- when a node is running low on a resource (commonly memory) and the kubelet needs to reclaim some by evicting entire Pods, it evicts in a specific, deliberate order: `BestEffort` Pods first (they made no reservation claim at all, so they're considered the least entitled to the node's capacity), then `Burstable` Pods (roughly in order of how far over their own requests they're currently running, so the ones consuming the most 'unreserved slack' go first), and `Guaranteed` Pods last, evicted only in genuinely extreme circumstances, since their usage was never supposed to be able to exceed what was explicitly reserved for them in the first place. The practical guidance: latency-sensitive or otherwise critical workloads should generally be `Guaranteed`, trading away some flexibility for the strongest protection against being evicted first when a node comes under pressure.

sections.heading: LimitRange and the Cost of Forgetting Limits Entirely
sections.body:
A `LimitRange` object, applied to a namespace, lets a cluster operator set default `requests`/`limits` for any container that doesn't specify its own, plus min/max bounds on what any container in that namespace is allowed to declare:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: default-limits
spec:
  limits:
    - type: Container
      default:
        cpu: 500m
        memory: 512Mi
      defaultRequest:
        cpu: 100m
        memory: 128Mi
      max:
        cpu: "2"
        memory: 2Gi
```

Without something like this in place, a container spec that simply forgets to declare `resources` at all doesn't fail or get rejected -- it silently becomes `BestEffort`, with zero reserved capacity from the scheduler's point of view and no ceiling on how much CPU or memory it can actually consume once running. This is a textbook 'noisy neighbor' setup: one forgotten `resources` block can let a single container consume unbounded memory on a node until it starves every other Pod sharing that node, entirely because nothing was ever declared to constrain it. A `LimitRange` closes this specific gap by giving every container in the namespace a sane default even when its author forgot to think about resources at all -- it's a safety net for exactly the class of mistake that's otherwise invisible until it causes an incident. Separately, the choice of setting `limits` far above `requests` cluster-wide (a deliberate overcommit strategy, betting that not every Pod will simultaneously need its full limit, for better average node utilization) versus setting `requests` equal to `limits` everywhere (fully reserved, `Guaranteed`, more predictable, but lower overall density) is a real cluster-wide capacity-planning tradeoff, not a one-size-fits-right-answer default.

examples.title: OOMKilled: Reading the Evidence in kubectl describe pod
examples.code:
kubectl describe pod web-abc123 | grep -A8 'Last State'
# Last State:     Terminated
#   Reason:       OOMKilled
#   Exit Code:    137
#   Started:      Tue, 12 Aug 2026 14:02:11 +0000
#   Finished:     Tue, 12 Aug 2026 14:04:47 +0000

kubectl get pod web-abc123
# NAME        READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
# web-abc123  1/1     Running   3          6m
examples.explanation: Exit Code: 137 and Reason: OOMKilled together are the unambiguous signature of a memory limit violation -- 137 decodes as 128 + 9 (SIGKILL), and OOMKilled specifically identifies the kernel's OOM killer as the thing that sent it, triggered because this container's cgroup hit its memory.limits ceiling and the kernel had no way to reclaim memory from it other than terminating the process outright. The RESTARTS: 3 in the second command confirms the kubelet has already restarted this container multiple times following exactly this pattern -- each restart gives the container a fresh chance to run, and if the underlying memory usage pattern (a leak, or simply a limit set too low for genuine peak usage) repeats, it will likely hit the same ceiling and get OOMKilled again, producing a slow-motion crash loop specifically caused by memory pressure rather than an application bug or a probe misconfiguration.

examples.title: CPU Throttling: Slow, Not Dead, and Invisible to RESTARTS
examples.code:
kubectl get pod web-abc123
# NAME        READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
# web-abc123  1/1     Running   0          2h
# -- Running, zero restarts, looks completely healthy from this view alone

kubectl top pod web-abc123
# NAME        CPU(cores)   MEMORY(bytes)
# web-abc123  500m         310Mi
# -- pinned exactly at its cpu limit (500m) for sustained periods, despite requests: 100m

# Application-level symptom: request latency has crept up 4x under moderate load,
# with no errors and no crashes anywhere in kubectl logs.
examples.explanation: Nothing in kubectl get pod or RESTARTS suggests any problem at all -- and that's exactly the trap with CPU throttling: it never kills anything, so none of the signals people reflexively check for 'is my Pod broken' (Running status, restart count, describe's Terminated/Reason fields) show anything unusual. kubectl top pod showing CPU usage pinned right at the configured limit (500m), combined with a pure latency degradation and zero errors, is the actual signature of throttling -- the container is being denied additional CPU time by the kernel's CFS bandwidth controller once it exhausts its quota for each accounting period, so every unit of work simply takes longer to complete, with no crash, no restart, and no log-visible error anywhere, because nothing about the process itself is malfunctioning.

examples.title: A LimitRange Filling In for a Forgotten resources Block
examples.code:
# Namespace has this LimitRange already applied:
# defaultRequest: { cpu: 100m, memory: 128Mi }
# default:        { cpu: 500m, memory: 512Mi }

# A developer submits this Pod spec with NO resources block at all:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: forgot-resources
spec:
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: my-app:1.0

# What actually gets scheduled and run (after the LimitRange's defaults are applied):
# containers:
#   - name: app
#     resources:
#       requests: { cpu: 100m, memory: 128Mi }
#       limits:   { cpu: 500m, memory: 512Mi }
examples.explanation: The developer's own spec declares nothing under resources at all -- left as-is, in a namespace with no LimitRange, this container would become BestEffort: zero reservation for the scheduler, and no ceiling on real usage at runtime. Because this namespace has a LimitRange with defaultRequest and default values configured, the API server's admission process fills in those values automatically at creation time, before the object is even persisted -- the container ends up Burstable (it has requests set, but they're not equal to its limits) with a sane 100m/128Mi reservation and a 500m/512Mi ceiling, entirely without the developer having to think about resource sizing for a first pass. This is exactly the safety net this concept describes: a namespace-wide default that prevents one forgotten resources block from becoming an unconstrained, unreserved container sharing a node with everything else.

misconceptions.description: Exceeding a CPU limit kills the container, the same way exceeding a memory limit does -- both are just "the resource ran out" in the same sense.
misconceptions.clarification: Only memory limit violations result in the container being killed (OOMKilled, exit code 137), because memory is incompressible -- there's no way to force a process to instantaneously use less RAM without actually terminating something. CPU time, by contrast, is compressible: the kernel's CFS bandwidth controller simply withholds additional CPU time from a container that has exhausted its quota for the current accounting period, which slows the container down (throttling) without touching its process at all. A CPU-limited container's RESTARTS count and Terminated/Reason fields stay completely unaffected by throttling -- the only visible symptom is degraded performance, checked via something like kubectl top or latency metrics, not anything in the Pod's lifecycle status.

misconceptions.description: If resources.requests isn't set on a container but resources.limits is, Kubernetes just uses the limits value as the request too, since that seems like the sensible default.
misconceptions.clarification: No such automatic behavior happens on its own -- if requests is omitted, the container is treated as requesting nothing at all for scheduling purposes, completely independent of whatever limits happens to say, unless a namespace has an explicit LimitRange configured with a defaultRequest value that the API server applies at admission time. Without a LimitRange in place, a container with only limits set (no requests) can be scheduled onto a node with zero regard for whether that node actually has enough free capacity to comfortably run it at its full limit, which is precisely the overcommit risk this concept describes.

exercises.prompt: A container has `requests: { memory: 128Mi }` and `limits: { memory: 256Mi }`. At runtime, its process tries to allocate memory until it's using 300Mi. What specifically happens, and what would `kubectl describe pod` show afterward?
hints: requests only affected the scheduler's placement decision, made once, before this container ever started running -- it plays no role in what happens now.
300Mi exceeds the LIMIT (256Mi), not just the request. Memory is incompressible -- what does the kernel do when a cgroup's memory limit is exceeded?
Think about the specific Reason and Exit Code kubectl describe pod reports for exactly this kind of termination.
exercises.expectedAnswer: The container is killed by the kernel's OOM killer the moment its actual usage tries to exceed the 256Mi limit -- the 128Mi request is irrelevant at this point, since it only mattered for scheduling. kubectl describe pod would show Last State: Terminated, Reason: OOMKilled, Exit Code: 137, and the kubelet would then restart the container per its restartPolicy, incrementing RESTARTS.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The 128Mi request was consumed entirely at scheduling time -- it played no role in this container's actual runtime behavior once it was placed on a node. What matters now is the 256Mi limit, enforced continuously by the kernel via the container's cgroup: memory is an incompressible resource, so there's no way for the kernel to force the process to simply use less RAM in the moment it tries to allocate past the limit. Instead, the OOM killer intervenes and sends SIGKILL, terminating the process outright. kubectl describe pod would report this precisely as Reason: OOMKilled with Exit Code: 137 (128 + signal 9), and depending on the Pod's restartPolicy (Always, by default, for Pods managed by a Deployment), the kubelet restarts the container afterward, which is what causes the RESTARTS count to climb -- and if the process's real memory needs genuinely exceed 256Mi under normal operation rather than as a one-off spike, this same OOMKilled cycle will very likely repeat indefinitely until the limit itself is raised or the application's memory usage is reduced.

exercises.prompt: A team reports their application has become mysteriously slow under load -- 4x higher latency than before -- but there are no errors in the logs, RESTARTS is 0, and the Pod has been continuously Running for hours with no crashes at all. Given this resources block, identify the likely cause and fix it.
exercises.code:
resources:
  requests:
    cpu: 100m
    memory: 256Mi
  limits:
    cpu: 100m
    memory: 512Mi
hints: No crashes and no restarts rules out OOMKilled entirely -- that leaves the OTHER resource dimension as the likely suspect.

cpu requests and cpu limits are set to the exact same value here (100m) -- what does that mean for how much CPU time this container is ever allowed to use, even briefly, even if the node has plenty of idle CPU sitting unused?
100m is a small fraction of a single core (0.1 CPU). Compare that against what a moderately loaded application would realistically need.
exercises.solutionCode:
resources:
  requests:
    cpu: 500m
    memory: 256Mi
  limits:
    cpu: 1000m
    memory: 512Mi
exercises.solutionExplanation: With cpu limits set to exactly 100m (one-tenth of a single core) and no crashes or restarts anywhere in the picture, this is a textbook CPU throttling symptom, not a memory or crash-related one: the container is being denied additional CPU time by the kernel's CFS bandwidth controller every time it exhausts its very small 100m-per-period quota, which manifests purely as slowness -- exactly the 4x latency increase reported -- with zero visibility in RESTARTS, Terminated reasons, or logs, since nothing about the process itself is failing. Raising the cpu limit substantially (to 1000m, a full core, here) gives the container real headroom to use more CPU time under load before hitting its ceiling and being throttled again, and raising cpu requests alongside it (to 500m) ensures the scheduler actually reserves enough CPU capacity on whichever node this Pod lands on to support that higher limit being used in practice, rather than relying on unreserved, potentially contended capacity to make the higher limit meaningful.

assessments.prompt: A Pod has one container with `requests: { cpu: 200m, memory: 256Mi }` and `limits: { cpu: 400m, memory: 256Mi }`. What QoS class does this Pod get, and why?
options: Guaranteed, because memory requests equal memory limits.
Burstable, because cpu requests (200m) do not equal cpu limits (400m), even though memory requests equal memory limits.
BestEffort, because at least one resource type (cpu) has a gap between requests and limits.
This is an invalid configuration and the Pod will be rejected by the API server.
assessments.explanation: Guaranteed requires requests to equal limits for BOTH cpu AND memory, across every container in the Pod -- here memory matches (256Mi == 256Mi) but cpu does not (200m requested vs. 400m limit), so the strict Guaranteed condition isn't met, and the Pod is classified as Burstable: it has requests set (ruling out BestEffort, which requires no requests or limits at all) but isn't fully requests-equals-limits (ruling out Guaranteed). Option A incorrectly treats matching on just one resource as sufficient for Guaranteed. Option C misapplies BestEffort, which specifically means no requests/limits declared at all, not merely an unequal pair. Option D is wrong -- having requests below limits for one resource while equal for another is a completely valid, common (Burstable) configuration, not a rejected one.

assessments.prompt: Explain, mechanistically, why exceeding a memory limit results in a container being killed while exceeding a CPU limit only results in the container being throttled, tracing the explanation down to the actual kernel-level behavior involved.
assessments.modelAnswer: The core distinction is whether the resource in question is compressible or incompressible. Memory is incompressible: at any given moment, a process either holds a certain amount of RAM or it doesn't, and there is no mechanism for the kernel to make a process instantaneously use less memory than it currently is without freeing something -- which the kernel cannot safely decide to do on the application's behalf, since it doesn't know which allocations are safe to discard. So when a container's cgroup memory usage reaches its configured limit and the process attempts to allocate further, the kernel's OOM killer intervenes and terminates the offending process outright with SIGKILL -- there's no intermediate state where the process is just 'slowed down' with respect to memory, only an on/off boundary that results in termination the moment it's crossed. Kubernetes reports this specific outcome as Reason: OOMKilled with Exit Code: 137 (the standard 128-plus-signal-number convention, with SIGKILL being signal 9). CPU, in sharp contrast, is compressible: it's fundamentally a measure of processing time over an interval, and a process can absolutely be given less of that time without being terminated -- it simply runs more slowly. CPU limits are enforced through the kernel's CFS (Completely Fair Scheduler) bandwidth controller, which tracks how much CPU time a container's cgroup has actually consumed within each short accounting period (commonly 100ms) and, once that period's quota is used up, simply declines to schedule that cgroup's processes for any additional CPU time until the next period begins. The process's memory, open file descriptors, network connections, and all other state remain completely untouched throughout -- it experiences repeated brief pauses in execution rather than any kind of termination, which Kubernetes calls throttling. This is exactly why the two failure modes look so different in practice: an OOMKilled container shows a clear Terminated/Reason/Exit Code signature and a climbing RESTARTS count, while a CPU-throttled container shows none of that at all -- Running, RESTARTS: 0, no errors in logs -- with the only visible symptom being degraded performance, detectable only by actually measuring CPU usage (pinned at the limit) or latency, not by anything in the Pod's basic status fields.
